title: Cyber Resilience Act - Reporting obligations (policy page)
date_evidence: Last update | 31 July 2026 | As of 11 September 2026, manufacturers are required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents impacting the security of products with digital elements.
key_claim: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must notify actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents: an early warning within 24 hours, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure (one month for incidents). They report once through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform to the CSIRT of their main establishment; the information is made available simultaneously to ENISA unless particularly exceptional circumstances apply; the receiving CSIRT shares it without delay with all other CSIRTs where the product is available, and may delay dissemination only on justified cybersecurity-related grounds under a delegated act adopted 11 December 2025. The platform will be operational by 11 September 2026 with functional and security testing under way.
frame_summary: The Commission presents the reporting duty as a simplification (report once, one platform) and as a routine next phase of CRA implementation, with the platform on schedule and the withholding exception tightly bounded.
verbatim_quote: The CSIRT initially receiving the notification will share without delay the notification with all the other CSIRTs on the territory of which the product with digital elements has been made available.
verbatim_list: Functional and security testing are under way.
In exceptional circumstances and based on justified cybersecurity-related grounds, the CSIRT may decide to delay dissemination to other CSIRTs
Manufacturers report only once through the CRA Single Reporting Platform (SRP).
They need to submit an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, and a full notification within 72 hours.

title: Commission publishes new guidance to support timely Cyber Resilience Act implementation (C(2026) 5252)
date_evidence: POLICY AND LEGISLATION | Publication 27 July 2026 | Last update 27 July 2026
key_claim: On 27 July 2026 the Commission published non-binding CRA guidance (Communication C(2026) 5252 and annex) covering scope, substantial modification, support periods and reporting obligations, with 67 practical examples aimed at microenterprises and SMEs; it restates that the main obligations apply from 11 December 2027 while reporting obligations apply as of 11 September 2026, and places the guidance within the Digital Omnibus simplification agenda.
frame_summary: The Commission frames the guidance as simplification in action and early support for smaller firms, positioning the September reporting start as something companies can prepare for confidently rather than as a compliance cliff.
verbatim_quote: Today's guidance - though non-binding - gives companies the clarity they need to prepare now, confidently and efficiently.
verbatim_list: The Cyber Resilience Act's main obligations apply from 11 December 2027, with reporting obligations already applying as of 11 September 2026.
with 67 practical examples, a range of use cases, flowcharts and graphs, ensuring that the path to compliance is clear and proportionate, without unnecessary administrative burden.
notes: Primary Commission news item with the guidance downloads. Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.

title: CRA Single Reporting Platform: Frequently Asked Questions (updated 4 September 2026)
date_evidence: Updated: 04 September 2026 | This page provides answers to frequently asked questions about the Cyber Resilience Act Single Reporting Platform (CRA SRP)
key_claim: The SRP is scheduled to be operational from 11 September 2026 and on that date will accept only mandatory Article 14 and 24 notifications, not voluntary reports; no API will be provided at initial release, so notifications go through the web interface; the public URL will be published before go-live; non-validated assigned representatives may submit up to 20 notifications before CSIRT validation becomes mandatory, and manufacturers are advised to register only when they need to submit; the obligation applies from 11 September 2026 to all in-scope products including those placed on the market before 11 December 2027, though not retrospectively to exploitation the manufacturer already knew of; ENISA will prepare biennial trend reports, the first within 24 months, and disclose fixed vulnerabilities to the European Vulnerability Database.
frame_summary: ENISA presents the platform as ready for a minimum viable launch and frames its constraints (no API, no voluntary channel, validation capacity) as staging decisions, asking manufacturers to hold back registration so national CSIRTs are not overloaded before day one.
verbatim_quote: However, no Application Programming Interface (API) will be provided at the initial release of the SRP, so notifications must be submitted through the platform interface.
verbatim_list: On the 11th of September the platform will ONLY allow the submission of mandatory reporting fulfilling Art 14 and 24(x). Voluntary reporting per art15 will not be possible.
Non-validated ARs may submit up to 20 notifications for one manufacturer before validation becomes mandatory.

title: Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026
date_evidence: Aug 31 2026 | The Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the CRA) enters its next implementation phase on 11 September 2026.
key_claim: The reporting obligations apply more than a year before most other CRA requirements and also cover products placed on the EU market before December 2027; the platform is not yet live and is expected to become operational on 11 September; under the Commission's 27 July 2026 guidance the clock starts when an initial assessment gives a 'reasonable degree of certainty' of active exploitation, and it does not stop at weekends or public holidays; CRA notifications must be coordinated with parallel NIS2 and GDPR duties until the Digital Omnibus consolidates channels.
frame_summary: Freshfields argues the short windows leave no room to build processes after an event, so manufacturers must fix ownership, escalation and cross-regime coordination now, treating the September date as the CRA's first operational test rather than a formality.
verbatim_quote: The reporting obligations also cover PDEs placed on the EU market before the CRA becomes fully applicable in December 2027.
verbatim_list: As practitioners will know from other EU reporting regimes, the clock does not stop at weekends or on public holidays.

this occurs when an initial assessment provides a “reasonable degree of certainty” that a vulnerability is being actively exploited or that a severe incident has occurred and compromised the PDE’s security.
The platform is not yet live and is expected to become operational on 11 September 2026.

title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Preparing for Vulnerability and Incident Reporting
date_evidence: Insights and Analysis | EU Cyber Resilience Act: Preparing for Vulnerability and Incident Reporting | 10 June 2026
key_claim: The reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 to all in-scope products made available on the EU market before full application (Article 69(3)); the SRP's single character is limited because the same event may also be reportable under GDPR, NIS2, DORA and contracts; non-compliance sits in the CRA's highest penalty tier, up to EUR 15,000,000 or 2.5% of worldwide turnover, though fines for missing the 24-hour deadline do not apply to microenterprises and small enterprises or to open-source stewards; API submission is not expected at go-live.
frame_summary: The firm argues the September duty forces manufacturers to inventory legacy products and fix the manufacturer role per product, and that the platform's 'single' reporting promise is narrower than it sounds because other regimes and contracts still run in parallel.
verbatim_quote: The SRP's "single" character is therefore limited.
verbatim_list: Notably, the reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 to all products with digital elements within the CRA's scope that have been made available on the EU market before full CRA application (Art. 69(3) CRA).

In particular, administrative fines do not apply to manufacturers that qualify as microenterprises or small enterprises for failures to meet the 24-hour early warning deadline, or to infringements by open-source software stewards (Art. 64(10) CRA).

non-compliance with the Art. 14 reporting obligations may lead to administrative fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or, for an undertaking, up to 2.5% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 64(2), Art. 71 CRA).
notes: Fetched via the hoganlovells.com URL, which redirects to the firm's hlc.com domain (publisher renamed Hogan Lovells Cadwalader); the canonical hlc.com URL is recorded. Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.

title: 24 Stunden für die erste Schwachstellenmeldung (German)
key_claim: German specialist IT press reports that the CRA becomes largely binding only at the end of 2027 but its reporting duties apply from 11 September 2026; not every discovered vulnerability triggers a report, only those with reliable evidence of active exploitation; the ENISA platform is not yet publicly available but is to be operational by 11 September; the Commission's late-July guidance is non-binding.
frame_summary: The magazine frames the duty as an operational readiness task for security and IT teams (who assesses, how affected products are identified, what information is assembled in the short windows), not as a legal novelty.
verbatim_quote: Nicht jede entdeckte Sicherheitslücke löst damit automatisch eine Meldepflicht aus: Voraussetzung sind belastbare Hinweise auf eine aktive Ausnutzung.
verbatim_list: Die Plattform ist derzeit noch nicht öffentlich verfügbar, soll aber spätestens zum 11. September betriebsbereit sein.

title: The CRA Readiness Reality: What Changed (and What Didn't) Between 2025 and 2026? (on the 2026 CRA Awareness and Readiness Report)
date_evidence: Angelah Liu | 19 June 2026 | The CRA Readiness Reality: What Changed (and What Didn’t) Between 2025 and 2026?
key_claim: The 2026 CRA Awareness and Readiness Report (843 respondents, 12,000-plus open-source projects) found 66% of respondents unfamiliar with the CRA, up from 62% in 2025, and 72% in the US and Canada; 32% produce SBOMs for all products; 51% rely passively on upstream projects for security fixes, up from 46%; 41% of manufacturers expect full compliance by December 2027; published CVEs across LFX-indexed projects rose 394% year on year in Q1 2026.
frame_summary: The foundation argues awareness campaigns have failed to move readiness and that the CRA makes upstream open-source contribution the economically rational compliance path, using the survey to promote its own courses, playbooks and working groups.
verbatim_quote: Far from narrowing, the awareness gap has widened: the proportion of respondents unfamiliar with the regulation rose to 66%, up from the 62% reported just one year prior (2026 report, p. 7).
verbatim_list: where 72% of respondents are unfamiliar with a regulation they'd need to comply with if their products with digital elements land in the EU market (2026 report, p. 8)

The share of respondents producing Software Bill of Materials (SBOMs) for all products held at 32%, and the share that passively rely on upstream projects for security fixes actually climbed, from 46% to 51% (2026 report, p. 13).
Time is running out, yet just 41% of manufacturers anticipate achieving total compliance by the December 2027 deadline.
Q1 2026 saw a 394% year-over-year increase in published CVEs, with high-severity vulnerabilities up 811% (2026 report, p. 24)
notes: Industry-foundation survey published with commercial sponsors (Balena, Ericsson, Revanite); Tier 4, used only as directional corroboration of readiness. Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.
